executiveSummary: This period featured several high-impact AI-enabled operations. A confirmed AI-assisted cyberattack disrupted European Commission applications in Brussels, underlining state and criminal interest in leveraging AI to amplify intrusion and disruption risks Source . Financially motivated actors continued to weaponize synthetic media at scale: Coinbase blocked approximately $4.7 million in attempted transfers tied to a deepfake Elon Musk livestream Source , while prosecutors detailed a $129 million executive-voice and attorney-impersonation scheme spanning multiple corporate sectors Source . Voice cloning and persona fabrication remain prominent. Authorities linked AI-generated "IT support" voice calls to ransomware intrusions affecting U.S. oil, healthcare, and industrial firms Source . OpenAI reported disrupting Russia- and Iran-linked false-front influence operations that deployed synthetic journalists, fabricated documents, and scripted audio Source . Separately, high-reach fabricated crisis narratives-including a fake Trump video-garnered tens of millions of views among U.S. and Spanish-speaking audiences Source . Legal and defensive measures are evolving. A lawsuit alleges unauthorized AI-generated endorsements using LeBron James's likeness Source . The EU published Article 50 guidelines clarifying deepfake disclosures Source , while new provenance tools and guidance were released by OpenAI and Microsoft Source Source . U.S. federal authorities also issued targeted election-security advisories on deepfake risks Security Advisory . Based on the number and severity of incidents across government, finance, corporate, media, and entertainment, the threat environment appears to be worsening, with real-time voice cloning and livestream deepfakes driving both operational disruptions and attempted high-dollar losses.
